costGuide.title: MG 84kWh EV Battery Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an 84kWh battery typically takes 6-10 hours at £75-£95/hr (specialist EV workshop) - the high‑voltage safety procedures, software calibration, and lifting equipment add complexity. [PATTERN DATA - based on typical EV battery replacement labour estimates]
paragraphs: (All figures . Fitted = supply price + labour band below.)

What genuinely moves the 84kWh replacement price is the battery's condition - state of health (SoH), cycle count, and whether any individual cells or modules can be reconditioned versus requiring a full pack replacement. The battery management system (BMS) must be properly calibrated to the new pack, which requires specialist diagnostic equipment. The age and mileage of the pack, plus its thermal history (whether it has been regularly fast‑charged), significantly affect value. See our full EV battery replacement cost guide.

failures.title: MG 84kWh EV Battery Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cell degradation and capacity loss - 80k-150k miles
items.onset: 80,000-150,000 miles [PATTERN DATA - expected for NMC lithium‑ion batteries]
items.whatHappens: Like all lithium‑ion batteries, the 84kWh pack gradually loses capacity over time and with use. The rate of degradation is influenced by: number of fast‑charge cycles, depth of discharge, temperature exposure, and age. Typical degradation is 1-2% per year, but heavy fast‑charging can accelerate this to 3-5% per year.
items.repairVsReplace: Individual cell or module replacement can restore capacity at £3,000-£6,000 if degradation is localised. If the entire pack is degraded beyond 70% SoH, full replacement is the only option.

items.title: Battery Management System (BMS) calibration issues - 40k-100k miles
items.onset: 40,000-100,000 miles [PATTERN DATA - reported on some EV platforms]
items.whatHappens: The BMS is the "brain" of the battery, managing cell balancing, thermal management, and state of charge calculations. Calibration drift can cause: inaccurate range estimates, reduced usable capacity (where the BMS limits charge), or error codes. This is often a software issue but can be triggered by uneven cell wear.
items.repairVsReplace: BMS recalibration typically costs £300-£800 at a specialist. Hardware BMS replacement costs £800-£2,000. This is rarely a pack‑replacement trigger.

items.title: Thermal management system failures - 50k-100k miles
items.onset: 50,000-100,000 miles [PATTERN DATA - common on liquid‑cooled EV batteries]
items.whatHappens: The 84kWh battery has an active liquid cooling and heating system to maintain optimal temperature. The cooling pump, hoses, or valves can fail, leading to battery overheating, derating, or in severe cases, degradation. This is more common on cars that have been regularly fast‑charged in hot conditions.
items.repairVsReplace: Cooling system repair costs £300-£800. If ignored, battery overheating can permanently damage cells, leading to full pack replacement.

failures.goodYearsLine: The 84kWh battery is considered a robust, well‑engineered pack when properly maintained. The NMC chemistry is mature and well‑understood. Regular battery health checks (not just range monitoring) are recommended from 60,000 miles onwards. Avoiding frequent 100% fast‑charging and keeping the battery between 20-80% for daily use significantly extends lifespan.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the 84kWh Battery
variants.intro: The 84kWh battery is MG's largest capacity pack, but MG also offers 51kWh, 64kWh, and 77kWh variants in different models and markets. The 84kWh is the long‑range option. Where to find the code: The battery capacity is printed on the battery pack label (visible from underneath the car) and appears on the V5C registration document under "Vehicle details" (battery capacity is now recorded on UK V5Cs). The car's infotainment system also displays battery capacity information. Which capacities get confused with it: The 84kWh is frequently confused with: - 64kWh - the medium‑range battery used in standard MG4 and MG ZS EV. This is a different pack with lower capacity and different cell count. - 77kWh - used in some MG4 models in other markets; not common in UK specification. - 51kWh - the entry‑level battery used in MG4 Standard Range. Significantly smaller and lighter. Why fitting the wrong variant matters: Battery packs are physically different sizes, weights, and mounting points. Fitting a 64kWh pack to an 84kWh car would require different mounting brackets, different BMS calibration, and could cause physical fitment issues. Always match the exact capacity and specification.

relatives.description: The entry‑level battery used in MG4 Standard Range models. It is significantly smaller (51kWh usable), lighter, and has a lower range (~220 miles). Physical dimensions and mounting points may differ - not interchangeable with the 84kWh pack.

The medium‑range battery used in MG4 Long Range and MG ZS EV standard range models. It has a different cell count and BMS calibration compared to the 84kWh pack. Not a straight swap without BMS reflashing and potentially different cooling system connections.

Used in some MG4 models in other markets (not common in UK specification). It sits between the 64kWh and 84kWh packs in capacity. Not relevant for UK owners but worth knowing if sourcing a used pack from Europe.
The same or similar 84kWh battery architecture is used in Roewe and Maxus models in China. Calibration and connectors may differ - not guaranteed to be a straight swap into an MG.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement 84kWh Battery - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used 84kWh battery makes sense only if the pack's state of health (SoH) is verified at 80%+ and it comes with a warranty. The key risks are: hidden degradation, BMS calibration mismatches, and thermal history (whether it has been regularly fast‑charged). Only buy from a reputable EV breaker who can provide diagnostic data and a warranty. This is a high‑risk, high‑reward purchase - a healthy used pack at £5,000-£8,000 can save thousands versus a new unit.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: The recommended route for most 84kWh battery replacements. A proper recon includes: cell health assessment, replacement of degraded cells/modules, new BMS calibration, and a full thermal system service. For a £8,000-£14,000 investment, you get a 12-24 month warranty and a battery that should be good for another 80k+ miles. This is the sensible choice for MG4 and ZS EV owners in the £10,000-£25,000 bracket.

options.label: New
options.body: A new 84kWh battery from MG or an authorised refurbisher is the ultimate peace‑of‑mind option, typically £12,000-£18,000+. It comes with manufacturer warranty and full capacity. This is only justified for high‑value cars where the owner plans to keep the vehicle for many years.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All our vetted specialists offer supply‑only, supply‑and‑fit, or full workshop installation. Fitting an EV battery requires specialist high‑voltage training, lifting equipment, and diagnostic tools - ensure your chosen garage is qualified for EV battery work. Fitting through the network includes a 12‑month warranty on parts and labour, with nationwide delivery to your chosen garage or home address.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The 84kWh battery is found in MG4 and MG ZS EV long‑range models, which typically hold values of £10,000-£25,000. A £8,000-£14,000 battery replacement may be a significant portion of the vehicle's value. For older or lower‑value examples (sub‑£12,000), consider the overall vehicle condition - if the battery is the only major issue, replacement may be justified; if there are other problems (bodywork, suspension, etc.), scrapping may be the better outcome. Always compare the total cost of battery + other repairs against the vehicle's market value.

items.question: How much does an MG 84kWh battery replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned 84kWh battery typically costs £8,000-£14,000 supply-only, with fitted prices ranging from £8,750-£15,250 depending on labour and warranty. Used units are cheaper at £5,000-£8,000 supply-only but carry higher risk of hidden degradation. A new battery can exceed £18,000+ supply-only. Fitting time is 6-10 hours at specialist EV workshop rates.

items.question: What is the most common failure on the 84kWh battery?
items.answer: The most common issue is gradual cell degradation, leading to capacity loss over time and mileage - typically 1-2% per year. BMS calibration issues and thermal management system failures are also reported but less common. Heavy fast-charging accelerates degradation - avoid frequent 100% DC fast charging. Regular battery health checks are recommended from 60,000 miles.

items.answer: The 84kWh battery is fitted to the MG4 Extended Range and the MG ZS EV Long Range. It is the largest capacity battery in MG's UK line-up, offering up to 323 miles of range. Standard-range and long-range MG4 models use 51kWh and 64kWh packs respectively. Standard-range MG ZS EV uses a 51kWh or 64kWh pack depending on the year.

items.question: Should I buy a used, reconditioned, or new 84kWh battery?
items.answer: For most owners, a reconditioned 84kWh battery is the better choice because it includes cell health assessment, replacement of degraded cells/modules, new BMS calibration, and a warranty. Used units are only advisable with verified state of health (80%+) and warranty. A new battery is only justified for high-value cars where long-term ownership is planned. Always buy from specialists with EV battery diagnostic equipment.

items.question: Is the 84kWh battery reliable overall?
items.answer: Yes, the 84kWh battery is considered a robust, well-engineered pack when properly maintained. The NMC chemistry is mature and well-understood. Regular battery health checks are recommended from 60,000 miles. Avoiding frequent 100% fast-charging significantly extends lifespan. Keeping the battery between 20-80% for daily use is the best practice.
